Mamdani’s slate of candidates with ties to the Democratic Socialists of America swept out area incumbent Democrats in a stunning win for the 34-year-old mayor.
Former New York City Comptroller Brad Lander unseated Representative Dan Goldman in a Lower Manhattan-area district, Assemblymember Claire Valdez defeated Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso in an open seat being vacated by retiring Representative Nydia Velazquez and activist Darializa Avila Chevalier narrowly defeated Representative Adriano Espaillat, a five-term congressman and head of the Hispanic Caucus.
All three are expected to win their elections in November, potentially complicating House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ role as the likely next speaker if Democrats win control of the House of Representatives.
Three new incoming congressional Democrats with no allegiance to the Democratic establishment will give Republicans new rhetorical ammunition to paint the party as radicals overtaken by socialism.
In addition to New York, Maryland and Utah both held primaries yesterday, in addition to a gubernatorial runoff in South Carolina.
Here’s what happened:
Mamdani vs Jeffries, House Dems
Three Mamdani-backed candidates won their House primaries last night, increasing the clout of the Democratic Socialists of America, which now claims several members of Congress, and expanding their influence over the left flank of the Democratic Party. The results were widely seen as shifting New York’s congressional delegation to the left, putting incumbents on notice that they are vulnerable if they are out of step with liberal voters who aren’t happy with centrist politics on immigration, Israel and Trump.
The question now is how these incoming members will fit into the House Democratic Caucus with a potentially narrow majority. Republicans have struggled to govern with razor-thin majorities in the House and Senate.
Mike Marinella, a spokesman for House Republicans’ campaign arm, called yesterday “the night the Democrat establishment officially surrendered to Zohran Mamdani and the socialist wing of their party.”
A ‘hellcat’ to take on Lawler
New York Democrats elevated combat veteran and national security expert Cait Conley, a member of the “Hellcat” group of female veterans running for office, to run against Republican Representative Mike Lawler in New York’s 17th, a swing district targeted by Democrats.
Lawler is considered the most vulnerable Republican in Congress, representing a district Democratic nominee Kamala Harris won in the 2024 presidential election, though Lawler has consistently performed well, twice winning a district that leans Democratic.
While the current political environment favours Democrats nationally, Lawler will begin the general election with a US$3 million (RM12.5 million) cash advantage over Conley.
Lasher wins expensive open seat
Assemblymember Micah Lasher beat Assemblymember Alex Bores in the crowded primary for the Democratic nomination to succeed retiring Representative Jerry Nadler in New York’s 12th Congressional District.
Kennedy scion Jack Schlossberg was a distant third, ahead of George Conway, a former Republican lawyer turned Trump critic whose ex-wife advised the president during his first term.
This district was the most expensive congressional primary race in New York, with tens of millions of dollars spent on advertising. Lasher will be the overwhelming favourite to be elected to Congress in November.

Mamdani’s Political Machine Flexes Its Muscle as DSA Candidates Score Major Primary Victories Across NYC
By: Fern Sidman
The political influence of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani expanded dramatically Tuesday night as a slate of progressive and Democratic Socialists of America-aligned congressional candidates notched significant victories in Democratic primary contests across New York City, signaling what many observers are already describing as a major realignment within the city’s Democratic Party.
According to report late of Tuesday night in The New York Post, the victories of Darializa Avila Chevalier, former City Comptroller Brad Lander, and State Assemblywoman Claire Valdez underscored the growing power of Mamdani’s political coalition and demonstrated the increasing influence of the Democratic Socialists of America movement within New York politics.
For supporters, the results represented validation of a progressive vision centered on affordability, housing reform, immigration protections, and a more confrontational stance toward traditional Democratic Party institutions. For critics, however, the outcome raised concerns about the continued leftward movement of the Democratic Party and the elevation of candidates whose views on Israel, immigration enforcement, and economic policy have frequently generated controversy.
At the center of the evening’s developments was the surprisingly strong performance of Darializa Avila Chevalier, who appeared poised to secure one of the most significant political upsets in recent New York history.
Late Tuesday evening, The New York Post reported that Avila Chevalier has prevailed over five-term incumbent Congressman Adriano Espaillat in New York’s 13th Congressional District, which encompasses portions of Upper Manhattan and the northwest Bronx.
With approximately 86% of votes counted, Avila Chevalier led Espaillat by a margin of 49.3% to 46%.
The advantage ultimately proved sufficient to prompt the veteran congressman to acknowledge defeat. “Tonight wasn’t our night,” Espaillat conceded as the results became increasingly difficult to overcome.
The outcome immediately drew comparisons to one of the most famous primary upsets in modern American politics. Political analysts quickly noted the similarities between Avila Chevalier’s apparent victory and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s stunning 2018 defeat of longtime Democratic leader Joe Crowley.
Like Ocasio-Cortez before her, Avila Chevalier successfully challenged an entrenched incumbent while positioning herself as a champion of grassroots progressive activism and Democratic Socialist priorities.
The symbolism was unmistakable. For many on the political left, the race represented further evidence that insurgent progressive candidates continue to possess significant appeal among Democratic primary voters, particularly in heavily Democratic urban districts. The broader significance of Tuesday’s results extended well beyond a single congressional contest.
The New York Post reported that Claire Valdez also secured victory in the race for New York’s 7th Congressional District. Valdez’s success was celebrated enthusiastically by supporters, with chants of “DSA! DSA!” reportedly erupting at her victory gathering in East Williamsburg.
The result further strengthened the possibility that the Democratic Socialists of America could significantly expand their representation in Congress. Currently, only two members of Congress—Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib—are formal members of the Democratic Socialists of America.
Should Avila Chevalier and Valdez ultimately prevail in general elections, that number could increase substantially. Mayor Mamdani’s role in these victories was impossible to ignore. Throughout the campaign season, he aggressively promoted the candidates, explicitly linking their success to his broader political agenda. Earlier on Election Day, Mamdani described the races as an opportunity for voters to elect partners who would help implement what he characterized as an “affordability agenda.”
“This is a moment when voters have the opportunity to vote in who would be a partner in fulfilling the affordability agenda,” Mamdani declared while campaigning alongside Brad Lander. That message resonated with many progressive voters frustrated by rising housing costs, inflationary pressures, and concerns regarding economic inequality.
Yet the victories also highlighted the increasingly ideological nature of New York City’s political landscape. The New York Post report emphasized that several of the victorious candidates have embraced policy positions that would have been considered far outside the Democratic mainstream only a few years ago.
Among the most controversial issues has been their stance toward Israel. Both Valdez and Avila Chevalier have been outspoken critics of Israeli policy and have characterized Israel’s military campaign in Gaza as genocide. Both candidates have also advocated ending American arms sales to Israel and support broader efforts aimed at distancing the United States from one of its closest Middle Eastern allies.
Those positions have generated significant support among certain segments of progressive voters while simultaneously provoking concern among pro-Israel Democrats and Jewish organizations.
The issue became particularly prominent during Avila Chevalier’s campaign. Her candidacy was repeatedly scrutinized because of past social media activity that critics characterized as inflammatory. According to The New York Post report, previously deleted posts resurfaced in which Avila Chevalier referred to the United States as “a f—ing disgrace,” criticized former President Joe Biden, and made statements regarding Israel that generated substantial controversy.
The revelations prompted significant backlash. Opponents argued the posts raised serious questions regarding her judgment and ideological orientation. Supporters countered that the statements reflected earlier periods of political activism and did not accurately represent her current positions.
Avila Chevalier herself sought to move beyond the controversy. She apologized for certain remarks and argued that critics were unfairly attempting to “re-litigate” positions she had since evolved beyond. Nevertheless, the issue remained a recurring feature of the campaign.
Tensions became particularly evident during a radio interview on Election Day when Avila Chevalier reportedly grew frustrated while facing questions about the social media posts and ultimately walked out of the interview. Despite those controversies, voters ultimately appeared willing to look beyond the disputes.
The election outcome suggests that concerns regarding affordability, housing, and broader dissatisfaction with establishment politics may have carried greater weight among many primary voters than controversies surrounding past statements. The success of Claire Valdez similarly reflected broader ideological shifts occurring within sections of the Democratic electorate.
The New York Post report noted that Valdez embraced policies closely aligned with Mamdani’s own political agenda. Among them was support for aggressive housing reforms, including proposals that critics have described as involving government seizure or intervention against problematic landlords. Supporters argue such measures are necessary to address chronic housing affordability issues and protect tenants.
Critics contend they represent excessive government intrusion into property rights. The debate highlights one of the defining political fault lines in contemporary urban politics.
Immigration policy also played a significant role. All three candidates supported abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Avila Chevalier reportedly went even further by expressing opposition to deporting certain foreign nationals convicted of crimes. Those positions are likely to become focal points in future debates as immigration continues to dominate national political discourse.
Brad Lander’s victory represented a somewhat different political trajectory. Although not formally affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America, Lander has increasingly aligned himself with the progressive movement. The New York Post report described how Lander strengthened his relationship with Mamdani following their political cooperation during previous electoral contests.
Over many years in New York politics, Lander cultivated a reputation as a progressive reformer. In recent years, however, he has become increasingly outspoken on issues involving campaign finance, economic inequality, and American foreign policy.
Following his victory, Lander reiterated criticisms of corporate political influence and argued that the United States should reconsider aspects of its relationship with Israel. “We shouldn’t be taking corporate PAC money from Wall Street and crypto and AI and AIPAC,” he stated during a post-election appearance. He added that “we have to reset the U.S. relationship with Israel.”
Those comments are likely to ensure that foreign policy remains a central issue as the new generation of progressive politicians seeks to reshape Democratic priorities. The victories also exposed divisions within traditionally progressive political circles. The New York Post reported that Mamdani’s endorsement decisions generated friction not only with establishment Democrats but also among certain allies within the broader progressive coalition.
One notable example involved the race for the district represented by retiring Congresswoman Nydia Velázquez.
Velázquez had backed Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso as her preferred successor., Although Reynoso himself supported Mamdani’s mayoral campaign, he was not aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America. Mamdani instead endorsed Valdez, creating tensions between different factions of the progressive movement.
The episode illustrated the increasingly complex alliances emerging within New York’s left-wing political landscape. As Tuesday’s results become fully digested, one conclusion appears increasingly difficult to dispute. Zohran Mamdani’s influence has expanded significantly beyond City Hall. His endorsements carried substantial weight. His political message resonated with voters. And his preferred candidates achieved notable success.
Whether these victories represent a lasting transformation of Democratic politics or simply another stage in the party’s ongoing ideological evolution remains uncertain.
What is clear is that Tuesday’s primaries marked a pivotal moment in New York City’s political history.
The victories of Avila Chevalier, Valdez, and Lander demonstrate that the coalition assembled by Mayor Mamdani possesses considerable political strength and growing confidence.
For supporters, the results represent a mandate for ambitious progressive change.
For opponents, they serve as a warning about the continued advance of policies they regard as too far outside the political mainstream.
Either way, the message delivered by Democratic primary voters was unmistakable: the political movement associated with Zohran Mamdani is no longer an insurgency on the margins.
It has become one of the most influential forces shaping the future direction of New York City politics
